entries.meaning: The two brothers thrill on hearing the letter, and the whole assembly especially delights in Bharata’s pure love. Daśaratha seats the messengers close and repeatedly asks whether the two boys—one dark, one fair, youthful, armed with bows and quivers, and travelling with Kauśika—are well. He asks how Janaka recognized them. Smiling, the envoys call Daśaratha the blessed jewel among kings because his sons Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa adorn the whole world.

The messengers say Daśaratha’s lion-like sons need no introduction, for their glory and power make the moon look dim and the sun cool; asking how they were recognized is like asking whether one needs a lamp to see the sun. They recount how unrivalled kings gathered for Sītā’s self-choice, yet none could move Śiva’s bow—not even Rāvaṇa, who once lifted Kailāsa. Then Rāma, jewel of Raghu’s line, broke it effortlessly, as an elephant snaps a lotus stalk.

words.grammar: perfective witness form describing the bow's effect on warriors' strength
epithet whose immediate referent is clarified by the following Kailāsa allusion

entries.meaning: The envoys continue: the enraged Paraśurāma arrived, threatened them in many ways, witnessed Rāma’s strength, handed him his own bow, and finally departed for the forest after repeated submission. Rāma’s strength is incomparable and Lakṣmaṇa is likewise a treasury of splendour; kings tremble before them like elephants before young lions. Daśaratha and the court relish this account, steeped in love, valour and glory. He tries to reward the envoys, but they cover their ears at the impropriety; he then gives Janaka’s letter to Vasiṣṭha and has the messengers respectfully tell the whole story.

Vasiṣṭha joyfully teaches that happiness covers the earth for the righteous: as rivers flow naturally to the sea though it desires nothing, wealth and joy come unbidden to people of dharma. He praises Daśaratha’s service to gurus, Brahmins, cows and gods, Kauśalyā’s purity, and the four sons’ courage, humility, vows and oceanic virtues. No one is more blessed than the father of a son like Rāma. He tells the king to sound the drums, prepare the wedding procession, and depart quickly.

Daśaratha summons the whole women’s palace and reads Janaka’s letter, then recounts the remaining events. The queens bloom with love like peahens hearing a raincloud; elder women bless the princes and the mothers sink into delight. They pass the dear letter from hand to hand, press it to their hearts, and repeatedly hear the king describe Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa’s fame. Calling it the sage’s grace, the king goes to the gate; the queens summon Brahmins, give joyful gifts, lavish offerings on petitioners, and bless Daśaratha’s four sons with long life and sovereignty.

Brahmins depart in fine garments, praising the princes, while great drums thunder. As the news spreads, congratulations arise in every home: Sītā, Janaka’s daughter, is to wed Raghubīra. Although auspicious Ayodhyā is always lovely, affection makes its new adornment lovelier still. Flags, banners, fabrics, fly-whisks, golden jars, arches, jewelled nets, turmeric, sacred grass, curds, rice and garlands fill the city; each house becomes auspicious, streets are sprinkled, and elegant courtyard designs are drawn.

Everywhere groups of women gather in complete new adornment, shining like lightning, with moonlike faces and fawn-like eyes whose beauty humbles Love’s own pride. Their melodious wedding songs shame the cuckoo. Daśaratha’s palace is transformed with an enchanting pavilion, auspicious articles, music, heralds’ praise, Vedic recitation and songs naming Rāma and Sītā. Joy seems to overflow the building in every direction; no poet can encompass the splendour of the house where Rāma, jewel upon all the gods’ crowns, took birth.

Daśaratha calls Bharata and orders horses, elephants and chariots made ready for Raghubīra’s wedding party. Thrilled, Bharata and Śatrughna summon all the cavalry captains, who hurry to fit richly chosen saddles upon excellent horses of many colours and breeds, so swift they seem eager to outfly the wind. Handsome young riders, peers of Bharata in age, mount in ornaments with bows, arrows and swords; two skilled swordsmen on foot accompany each horseman.

words.grammar: nominal comparison in the image of the horses striking the ground

entries.meaning: The proven warriors assemble outside the city and display their horses’ many gaits to the beat of drums. Charioteers decorate magnificent chariots with flags, banners, gems, ornaments, fly-whisks and tinkling bells bright enough to rival the sun. Countless noble horses are yoked, including ones said to cross water as if it were land, without a hoof sinking and at extraordinary speed. Weapons and equipment are made ready, warriors are summoned, and the wedding procession begins to gather amid good omens for every traveller’s purpose.

Splendid howdahs are set upon richly adorned elephants, whose bells make the rutting animals resemble a beautiful bank of monsoon clouds. Brahmin groups ride in palanquins and comfortable seats, as though all the Vedic metres had taken bodily form. Bards, heralds, singers, mules, camels and oxen join them; innumerable bearers carry countless goods in shoulder-yokes, and every servant forms his own well-equipped company. Hearts brim with joy and bodies thrill at the thought of soon seeing the heroes Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
